title: CTS Radical Christianity — Unit 3: Love God

blocks.en: 📖 Radical Christianity: The Ten Commandments of Jesus — Unit 3: Love God
blocks.es_reference: 📖 Cristianismo Radical: Los Diez Mandamientos de Jesús — Unidad 3: Amar a Dios

blocks.en: Professor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: "You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind." — Matthew 22:37 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Amarás al Señor tu Dios con todo tu corazón, y con toda tu alma, y con toda tu mente." — Mateo 22:37 (RVG)

blocks.en: 1. The Question That Exposes the Heart
blocks.es_reference: 1. La Pregunta Que Desnuda el Corazón

blocks.en: Matthew 22:34-38 (NKJV): "But when the Pharisees heard that He had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. Then one of them, a lawyer, asked Him a question, testing Him, and saying, 'Teacher, which is the great commandment in the law?' Jesus said to him, 'You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the first and great commandment.'"
blocks.es_reference: Mateo 22:34-38 (RVG): "Pero los fariseos, oyendo que había hecho callar a los saduceos, se juntaron a una. Y uno de ellos, intérprete de la ley, preguntó por tentarle, diciendo: Maestro, ¿cuál es el gran mandamiento en la ley? Jesús le dijo: Amarás al Señor tu Dios con todo tu corazón, y con toda tu alma, y con toda tu mente. Éste es el primero y grande mandamiento."

blocks.en: The man who asked was an expert in the law, and the text says plainly he asked in order to test Jesus, not to learn from Him. The rabbis loved to argue over which of the six hundred and thirteen commands stood highest, hoping to catch a teacher in a careless ranking. Jesus did not take the bait, and He did not hesitate. He reached back to the Shema, the confession every faithful Jew recited daily from Deuteronomy 6, and named love for God as the first and greatest commandment of all.
blocks.es_reference: El que preguntó era un intérprete de la ley, y el texto dice con claridad que preguntó para tentar a Jesús, no para aprender de Él. A los rabinos les encantaba discutir cuál de los seiscientos trece mandamientos era el más alto, con la esperanza de atrapar a un maestro en una clasificación descuidada. Jesús no cayó en la trampa, y no vaciló. Se remontó al Shemá, la confesión que todo judío fiel recitaba a diario en Deuteronomio 6, y nombró el amor a Dios como el primero y más grande mandamiento de todos.

blocks.en: Notice what that answer does. It moves the whole question off the surface of outward rule-keeping and drives it down to the heart. The greatest thing God requires is not a performance He can audit but an affection: love, given with the whole self. That is the foundation this entire course is built on, and it is the foundation of the Christian life. Get this command right and the others have somewhere to grow from; get it wrong and every other command becomes a burden.
blocks.es_reference: Note lo que hace esa respuesta. Aparta toda la cuestión de la superficie del cumplimiento externo de reglas y la lleva al fondo, al corazón. Lo más grande que Dios requiere no es una actuación que Él pueda auditar, sino un afecto: el amor, dado con todo el ser. Ese es el fundamento sobre el cual se edifica todo este curso, y es el fundamento de la vida cristiana. Acierte en este mandamiento y los demás tendrán de dónde crecer; equivóquese, y todo otro mandamiento se vuelve una carga.

blocks.en: 2. A Love That Is Total, and a Love of Degree
blocks.es_reference: 2. Un Amor Total, y un Amor de Grado

blocks.en: This passage tells us that the very foundation of Christianity is the love of God. That is an easy thing to talk about — anyone can say "I love the Lord," and many do, inside the church and out. But Jesus attaches conditions to the kind of love He means, and the first is that it must be total. Christianity is a religion of the whole person. You are to love God with all your heart, all your soul, and all your mind — every faculty bent toward Him. The three are not separate compartments to be ticked off but three angles on one undivided self, and together they leave no part of a person exempt.
blocks.es_reference: Este pasaje nos dice que el fundamento mismo del cristianismo es el amor de Dios. Eso es algo fácil de decir — cualquiera puede decir "amo al Señor," y muchos lo hacen, dentro de la iglesia y fuera. Pero Jesús pone condiciones a la clase de amor que quiere decir, y la primera es que debe ser total. El cristianismo es una religión del hombre entero. Has de amar a Dios con todo tu corazón, toda tu alma y toda tu mente — cada facultad inclinada hacia Él. Los tres no son compartimentos separados que tachar, sino tres ángulos de un solo ser indiviso, y juntos no dejan exenta ninguna parte de la persona.

blocks.en: This total love is the very basis of obedience. When you love God with everything, you strive with everything within you to do what He wants; obedience stops being a demand imposed from outside and becomes the natural leaning of a life. Just as a tree that grows by the seashore is bent over the years in the direction of the prevailing wind, the whole of the Christian is meant to be bent, steadily and permanently, by the will of God. And there is a second condition: this is a love of degree. God has given us many good things to enjoy in this world, and they are gifts. But we must always guard the order of our loves, so that no gift — however good — ever becomes as important to us as the Giver. If we love God with all our heart and soul and mind, then nothing is allowed to come between us and Him.
blocks.es_reference: Este amor total es la base misma de la obediencia. Cuando amas a Dios con todo, te esfuerzas con todo lo que hay dentro de ti por hacer lo que Él quiere; la obediencia deja de ser una exigencia impuesta desde afuera y se vuelve la inclinación natural de una vida. Así como un árbol que crece junto a la orilla del mar se va doblando con los años en la dirección del viento que predomina, todo el cristiano ha de ser doblado, firme y permanentemente, por la voluntad de Dios. Y hay una segunda condición: éste es un amor de grado. Dios nos ha dado muchas cosas buenas para disfrutar en este mundo, y son regalos. Pero siempre debemos guardar el orden de nuestros amores, de modo que ningún regalo — por bueno que sea — llegue a ser tan importante para nosotros como el Dador. Si amamos a Dios con todo el corazón, el alma y la mente, entonces nada se permite que se interponga entre nosotros y Él.

blocks.en: 3. Called to Love, Not Merely to Serve
blocks.es_reference: 3. Llamados a Amar, No Solo a Servir

blocks.en: We as Christians sometimes miss the forest for the trees. We pick up the idea that all God really wants from us is to work ourselves to death for Him, and so we become guilt-ridden, working our fingers to the bone and ending up miserable. We even inscribe it on our bulletins and hang it over our doors: "Called to serve." But that motto, taken first, is wrong. We are not first called to serve at all; we are called to love. Service is good in its place, but it is meant to grow out of love, never to replace it — and when we reverse the order, religion turns into joyless duty.
blocks.es_reference: Los cristianos a veces no vemos el bosque por los árboles. Adoptamos la idea de que todo lo que Dios de veras quiere de nosotros es que nos matemos trabajando para Él, y así nos volvemos cargados de culpa, trabajando hasta el agotamiento y terminando miserables. Hasta lo inscribimos en nuestros boletines y lo colgamos sobre nuestras puertas: "Llamados a servir." Pero ese lema, tomado primero, está equivocado. No somos llamados primero a servir; somos llamados a amar. El servicio es bueno en su lugar, pero ha de brotar del amor, nunca reemplazarlo — y cuando invertimos el orden, la religión se vuelve un deber sin gozo.

blocks.en: Scripture gives us one quiet model of this. Of Enoch almost nothing is recorded except the one thing that matters most: he walked with God, and God took him. What a commentary on a life — that the sum of it is friendship with God. Enoch was one of the few who actually fulfilled the purpose for which we were all made, for God created us for fellowship with Himself. The searching question for us is simple: to this point, would the commentary of my life read, "He walked with God"?
blocks.es_reference: La Escritura nos da un modelo callado de esto. De Enoc casi nada se registra salvo lo único que más importa: caminó con Dios, y Dios lo llevó consigo. Qué comentario sobre una vida — que la suma de ella es la amistad con Dios. Enoc fue uno de los pocos que de veras cumplió el propósito para el cual todos fuimos hechos, pues Dios nos creó para tener comunión con Él mismo. La pregunta que escudriña es sencilla: hasta ahora, ¿diría el comentario de mi vida: "Caminó con Dios"?

blocks.en: 4. The Greatest Commandment and the Greatest Sin
blocks.es_reference: 4. El Mandamiento Más Grande y el Pecado Más Grande

blocks.en: Have you ever thought about what the greatest sin actually is? We all keep a private list — murder near the top, then adultery, theft, lying, blasphemy, the sins whose weight we feel instinctively. But none of these is the biggest. As Peter Lord points out, the greatest sin is most likely tied to the greatest commandment, for to commit the greatest sin is simply to break the greatest commandment. If loving God with everything is first, then failing to love Him is the first and greatest sin — and it is precisely the one we never think to put on our list.
blocks.es_reference: ¿Ha pensado alguna vez cuál es de veras el pecado más grande? Todos guardamos una lista privada — el homicidio cerca de la cima, luego el adulterio, el robo, la mentira, la blasfemia, los pecados cuyo peso sentimos por instinto. Pero ninguno de estos es el más grande. Como señala Peter Lord, el pecado más grande está muy probablemente ligado al mandamiento más grande, pues cometer el pecado más grande es sencillamente quebrantar el mandamiento más grande. Si amar a Dios con todo es lo primero, entonces no amarlo es el primero y más grande pecado — y es justamente el que nunca pensamos en poner en nuestra lista.

blocks.en: This reframes everything God asks of us. What God has been most interested in from the very beginning is not our work — He has all power and needs no help from us — nor our money, since He already owns everything that exists. What He cares about is our fellowship, our love. If we work for God without loving God, the whole enterprise becomes a grinding struggle instead of a joy. The test of it is prayer: it is hard to stay even five minutes before the Father unless there is a real love relationship underneath. We read of saints who rose at three in the morning to pray for hours, and we have to wonder whether they were driven by guilt or whether they simply loved God far more than we do. The honest desire of a Christian heart is to love God with the whole of life.
blocks.es_reference: Esto replantea todo lo que Dios nos pide. Lo que más le ha interesado a Dios desde el mismísimo principio no es nuestro trabajo — Él tiene todo el poder y no necesita ayuda nuestra — ni nuestro dinero, pues ya posee todo lo que existe. Lo que le importa es nuestra comunión, nuestro amor. Si trabajamos para Dios sin amar a Dios, todo el empeño se vuelve una lucha agotadora en lugar de un gozo. La prueba está en la oración: cuesta quedarse siquiera cinco minutos delante del Padre si no hay debajo una verdadera relación de amor. Leemos de santos que se levantaban a las tres de la mañana a orar por horas, y tenemos que preguntarnos si los impulsaba la culpa o si sencillamente amaban a Dios mucho más que nosotros. El deseo honesto de un corazón cristiano es amar a Dios con la totalidad de la vida.

blocks.en: 5. Loving God More Than Family
blocks.es_reference: 5. Amar a Dios Más Que a la Familia

blocks.en: If that love is total, it will sometimes be tested against our other loves — and Jesus named the hardest one first. "Anyone who loves father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me," He said, "and anyone who loves son or daughter more than Me is not worthy of Me" (Matthew 10:37). We rightly honor devotion to family; love within a family is one of God's good gifts. But precisely because it is so good, it carries a real danger: that we come to love even something as worthy as our family more than we love God. Sometimes God will ask us to settle which love is first.
blocks.es_reference: Si ese amor es total, a veces será probado frente a nuestros otros amores — y Jesús nombró primero el más difícil. "El que ama a padre o madre más que a mí, no es digno de mí," dijo, "y el que ama a hijo o hija más que a mí, no es digno de mí" (Mateo 10:37). Con razón honramos la devoción a la familia; el amor dentro de la familia es uno de los buenos regalos de Dios. Pero precisamente por ser tan bueno, lleva un peligro real: que lleguemos a amar incluso algo tan digno como nuestra familia más de lo que amamos a Dios. A veces Dios nos pedirá que resolvamos cuál amor es primero.

blocks.en: Abraham faced that test in its sharpest form when God asked him to offer Isaac, the son he had waited a lifetime for. He loved the boy more than his own life — yet he loved God more, and in heart and intent he gave his son to the Lord. God never meant for the knife to fall; He stayed Abraham's hand. The point was never the death of Isaac but the discovery of where Abraham's first love lay. The same test comes to us in quieter forms: family attachments and family concerns can quietly hold back a life of obedience.
blocks.es_reference: Abraham enfrentó esa prueba en su forma más aguda cuando Dios le pidió ofrecer a Isaac, el hijo que había esperado toda una vida. Amaba al muchacho más que a su propia vida — y sin embargo amaba más a Dios, y de corazón y en intención entregó a su hijo al Señor. Dios nunca quiso que el cuchillo cayera; detuvo la mano de Abraham. El punto nunca fue la muerte de Isaac sino el descubrimiento de dónde estaba el primer amor de Abraham. La misma prueba nos llega en formas más calladas: los apegos y las preocupaciones familiares pueden frenar discretamente una vida de obediencia.

blocks.en: Bunyan and the Welches: John Bunyan, imprisoned in England for preaching, was less troubled for himself than for his family, and especially his blind daughter — yet he knew he must obey God, and said, "I must do it." John Welch, a nonconformist preacher in Scotland, was jailed for the gospel until the dampness of the underground cell broke his health. When his wife Mary begged the king for his release, the king answered that he would free him if she would promise her husband would never preach again. She held up her apron and said she would rather have her husband's head in it than make such a promise. She loved her husband — but she loved God more.
blocks.es_reference: Bunyan y los Welch: John Bunyan, encarcelado en Inglaterra por predicar, se angustiaba menos por sí mismo que por su familia, y en especial por su hija ciega — pero sabía que debía obedecer a Dios, y dijo: "Debo hacerlo." John Welch, predicador inconformista en Escocia, fue encarcelado por el evangelio hasta que la humedad de la celda subterránea quebró su salud. Cuando su esposa Mary suplicó al rey por su libertad, el rey respondió que lo soltaría si ella prometía que su marido nunca volvería a predicar. Ella levantó su delantal y dijo que prefería tener en él la cabeza de su esposo antes que hacer tal promesa. Amaba a su esposo — pero amaba más a Dios.

blocks.en: 6. Loving God More Than Money
blocks.es_reference: 6. Amar a Dios Más Que al Dinero

blocks.en: The second rival love Jesus named is money. "You cannot serve God and money," He said, and one of His hardest words was spoken to a rich young ruler who sensed something was missing and asked how to inherit eternal life. Jesus saw that the man loved his wealth more than he loved God — that money had quietly become his god, claiming his time, thought, and energy — and so He put His finger exactly there: sell what you have, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. It was the one thing the young man could not do, and he went away sorrowful.
blocks.es_reference: El segundo amor rival que Jesús nombró es el dinero. "No podéis servir a Dios y a las riquezas," dijo, y una de sus palabras más duras se la dijo a un joven rico que presentía que algo le faltaba y preguntó cómo heredar la vida eterna. Jesús vio que el hombre amaba su riqueza más de lo que amaba a Dios — que el dinero se había vuelto calladamente su dios, reclamando su tiempo, su pensamiento y su energía — y por eso puso el dedo justo allí: vende lo que tienes, dalo a los pobres, y tendrás tesoro en el cielo. Era lo único que el joven no podía hacer, y se fue triste.

blocks.en: The question that story presses on us is one of ownership: who really owns what we hold? If it is mine, I will use it one way; if it is God's, I will use it another. Scripture answers plainly — the earth, the cattle, even the birds belong to God, and He owns all that we have. He is generous in letting us use His possessions and does not demand them all back, but He does say that the tithe is the Lord's. To withhold it is not thrift; it is to rob God. We give our tithes and offerings for a reason: so that Christ may be known, so that people are saved and taught here, and so that others can be sent out to tell the world of the Savior. It is a glorious privilege to have a part in that work, and how we hold our money quietly reveals whether we love the gift or the Giver.
blocks.es_reference: La pregunta que esa historia nos plantea es de propiedad: ¿quién posee de veras lo que tenemos? Si es mío, lo usaré de una manera; si es de Dios, lo usaré de otra. La Escritura responde con claridad — la tierra, el ganado, hasta las aves pertenecen a Dios, y Él posee todo lo que tenemos. Es generoso al dejarnos usar sus posesiones y no las exige todas de vuelta, pero sí dice que el diezmo es del Señor. Retenerlo no es ahorro; es robar a Dios. Damos nuestros diezmos y ofrendas por una razón: para que Cristo sea conocido, para que aquí la gente sea salva y enseñada, y para que otros sean enviados a anunciar al mundo del Salvador. Es un privilegio glorioso tener parte en esa obra, y cómo manejamos nuestro dinero revela calladamente si amamos el regalo o al Dador.

blocks.en: The Brazilian family: Deep in the interior of Brazil a blacksmith was converted by an open-air evangelist, given a Bible, and went home and taught his family from it for years. When Baptist workers finally found them, they discovered the family had been setting aside a tenth of their cattle earnings the whole time, simply because the Scriptures said the tithe belonged to God. They had never even seen a church — yet they had proved, with their herd, that they loved God more than money.
blocks.es_reference: La familia brasileña: En el interior profundo de Brasil un herrero fue convertido por un evangelista al aire libre, recibió una Biblia, y volvió a casa y enseñó a su familia de ella por años. Cuando unos obreros bautistas por fin los hallaron, descubrieron que la familia había estado apartando todo ese tiempo la décima parte de sus ganancias del ganado, sencillamente porque las Escrituras decían que el diezmo pertenecía a Dios. Nunca habían visto siquiera una iglesia — y sin embargo habían probado, con su rebaño, que amaban a Dios más que al dinero.

blocks.en: 7. Looking to Him More Than to Life
blocks.es_reference: 7. Mirar a Él Más Que a la Vida

blocks.en: To love God above family and money finally comes down to keeping our eyes on Him above everything, including our own life and desires. Hebrews 12:2 puts the whole Christian life in three words: "looking unto Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith." The instruction is simple and somehow the hardest thing to keep doing. Many of us came to trust Christ early and meant to keep our eyes on Him for life, yet somewhere we looked away. It is like the children's game of staring until someone blinks; in our spiritual lives we blink, lose sight of the Lord, and look somewhere else — usually toward the glitter, power, and desires the world holds out.
blocks.es_reference: Amar a Dios por encima de la familia y del dinero al fin se reduce a mantener los ojos en Él por encima de todo, incluso de nuestra propia vida y nuestros deseos. Hebreos 12:2 resume toda la vida cristiana en tres palabras: "puestos los ojos en Jesús, el autor y consumador de la fe." La instrucción es sencilla y de algún modo lo más difícil de seguir haciendo. Muchos vinimos a confiar en Cristo temprano y quisimos tener los ojos en Él toda la vida, y sin embargo en algún punto miramos a otro lado. Es como el juego de niños de mirarse fijamente hasta que alguien parpadea; en nuestra vida espiritual parpadeamos, perdemos de vista al Señor, y miramos a otra parte — por lo general hacia el brillo, el poder y los deseos que el mundo ofrece.

blocks.en: David is the great example of a man who blinked. As a shepherd boy his faith was so strong that, armed with a sling and his trust in God, he brought down a giant the whole army feared. God made him king, and nothing on earth could stand against such a man. But then David looked away — caught up in ruling, in power, in everyone telling him how great he was — and one evening his gaze drifted to his neighbor's wife, and he fell. Had his eyes stayed on the Lord, he could have escaped the temptation altogether. So can we. The struggle of the Christian life is largely a struggle of where we are looking, and the everyday things we walk right past can be exactly where God is waiting to be seen.
blocks.es_reference: David es el gran ejemplo de un hombre que parpadeó. De muchacho pastor su fe era tan fuerte que, armado de una honda y de su confianza en Dios, derribó a un gigante al que todo el ejército temía. Dios lo hizo rey, y nada en la tierra podía oponerse a tal hombre. Pero entonces David miró a otro lado — absorto en gobernar, en el poder, en que todos le dijeran cuán grande era — y una tarde su mirada se desvió a la mujer de su prójimo, y cayó. Si sus ojos hubieran seguido en el Señor, habría escapado por completo de la tentación. Nosotros también podemos. La lucha de la vida cristiana es en gran medida una lucha sobre hacia dónde miramos, y las cosas cotidianas junto a las que pasamos de largo pueden ser justo donde Dios espera ser visto.

blocks.en: The ten-dollar bill: Walking home one windy evening, our family passed a scrap of paper on the ground. It did not register with me; my wife Andi even kicked it aside. But our youngest son, Aaron, picked it up — "Wow, ten dollars!" We had all seen the very same thing, yet only the one who truly looked recognized it for what it was.
blocks.es_reference: El billete de diez dólares: Volviendo a casa una tarde de viento, nuestra familia pasó junto a un papelito en el suelo. A mí no me registró; mi esposa Andi hasta lo apartó de una patada. Pero nuestro hijo menor, Aaron, lo recogió — "¡Guau, diez dólares!" Todos habíamos visto exactamente lo mismo, pero solo el que de veras miró lo reconoció por lo que era.

blocks.en: 8. Never Too Early and Never Too Late to Look
blocks.es_reference: 8. Nunca Demasiado Temprano ni Demasiado Tarde para Mirar

blocks.en: If the whole of it is learning to look to Jesus, then two encouragements follow. First, it is never too early to begin. Many of the great men and women of God fixed their eyes on Christ when they were young, and a single steady look at Him can set the whole course of a life. The lay preacher in a snowbound English chapel who could only repeat one verse — "Look unto Me, and be saved" — and pressed it on a miserable fifteen-year-old, was used that day to turn the boy who became Charles Spurgeon into a Christian. A young heart that learns to look to Jesus has been given the best of all beginnings.
blocks.es_reference: Si todo se reduce a aprender a mirar a Jesús, entonces se siguen dos alientos. Primero, nunca es demasiado temprano para empezar. Muchos de los grandes hombres y mujeres de Dios fijaron sus ojos en Cristo siendo jóvenes, y una sola mirada firme a Él puede fijar el rumbo entero de una vida. Aquel predicador laico, en una capilla inglesa cubierta de nieve, que solo podía repetir un versículo — "Mirad a mí, y sed salvos" — y se lo insistió a un muchacho miserable de quince años, fue usado ese día para convertir al joven que llegó a ser Charles Spurgeon. Un corazón joven que aprende a mirar a Jesús ha recibido el mejor de los comienzos.

blocks.en: Second, it is never too late. There have been people with great sin behind them and grey hair on their heads who at last looked to Jesus alone and were received, for the opportunity stands open regardless of how a person has lived. B. H. Carroll, godless and embittered and crippled by war, was dragged unwillingly to church by his mother; the sermon left him empty, but at its end a light from heaven seemed to break, Christ stood before him calling, and he looked up once and forever and became a great man of God. Whether we come early or late, the command is the same and the door is the same: love God with all your heart, and keep looking to Him until, as the old hymn says, the things of earth grow strangely dim in the light of His glory and grace. Loving God is the first and greatest commandment — and it begins, and is kept, by looking to Him.
blocks.es_reference: Segundo, nunca es demasiado tarde. Ha habido personas con grandes pecados a sus espaldas y canas en la cabeza que al fin miraron a Jesús solamente y fueron recibidas, pues la oportunidad queda abierta sin importar cómo haya vivido uno. B. H. Carroll, impío y amargado y lisiado por la guerra, fue llevado a la iglesia por su madre contra su voluntad; el sermón lo dejó vacío, pero al final una luz del cielo pareció romper, Cristo se puso delante de él llamándolo, y miró hacia arriba de una vez y para siempre, y llegó a ser un gran hombre de Dios. Sea que vengamos temprano o tarde, el mandamiento es el mismo y la puerta es la misma: ama a Dios con todo tu corazón, y sigue mirando a Él hasta que, como dice el viejo himno, las cosas de la tierra se vuelvan extrañamente tenues a la luz de su gloria y su gracia. Amar a Dios es el primero y más grande mandamiento — y comienza, y se mantiene, mirando a Él.

mc.stem: In Matthew 22, why did the lawyer ask Jesus which was the greatest commandment?
options: He was testing Jesus, hoping to trap Him
He genuinely wanted to learn from Jesus
He had forgotten the commandments
He was sent by the Sadducees
mc.why: The text says he asked 'testing Him' — the rabbis loved to trap a teacher in a careless ranking of the 613 commands.

mc.stem: What did Jesus name as the first and greatest commandment?
options: Do not murder
Keep the Sabbath holy
Love your neighbor as yourself
Love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, and mind
mc.why: Jesus reached back to the Shema (Deut 6) and named love for God with all the heart, soul, and mind as the first and greatest.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, what does it mean that this love must be 'total'?
options: It means loving God only on Sundays
It means feeling intense emotion
It means the whole person — every faculty — is bent toward God
It means giving God ten percent
mc.why: Christianity is a religion of the whole person; heart, soul, and mind are three angles on one undivided self, leaving no part exempt.

mc.stem: What image does the lesson use for how the whole Christian should be shaped by God's will?
options: A river carving a canyon
A seashore tree bent by the prevailing wind
A lamp on a stand
A house built on rock
mc.why: As a seashore tree is bent over the years by the prevailing wind, the whole Christian is meant to be bent by the will of God.

mc.stem: The lesson says this love is also a love of 'degree.' What danger does that guard against?
options: Letting a good gift become as important to us as God Himself
Loving God too intensely
Spending too much time in prayer
Giving away too much money
mc.why: God gives many good gifts, but we must guard the order of our loves so no gift ever becomes as important to us as the Giver.

mc.stem: The lesson challenges a common church motto. Which one, and what correction is given?
options: 'God is love' — we should fear Him instead
'Jesus saves' — we must save ourselves
'Called to serve' — we are first called to love, not merely to serve
'Give generously' — we should keep what we earn
mc.why: We inscribe 'Called to serve' over our doors, but service must grow out of love; we are first called to love, not merely to serve.

mc.stem: What is nearly the entire biblical record of Enoch's life, and why does it matter?
options: He built an ark; it shows obedience
He led Israel; it shows leadership
He wrote many psalms; it shows worship
He walked with God, and God took him; it shows we are made for fellowship with God
mc.why: Almost all Scripture says of Enoch is that he walked with God and God took him — a model of the fellowship we were created for.

mc.stem: According to the lesson (citing Peter Lord), what is most likely the greatest sin?
options: Murder
Failing to love God — breaking the greatest commandment
Blasphemy
Theft
mc.why: Since to commit the greatest sin is to break the greatest commandment, failing to love God is the first and greatest sin — the one we never list.

mc.stem: The lesson says God is not most interested in our work or our money. Why not?
options: Because He has all power and already owns everything; He wants our fellowship and love
Because work and money are sinful
Because He cannot use them
Because only prayer matters to Him
mc.why: God has all power and owns everything, so He needs neither our work nor money; what He desires is our fellowship and love.

mc.stem: Which command did Jesus give about loving God versus family (Matthew 10:37)?
options: Honor your father and mother above all
Anyone who loves father, mother, son, or daughter more than Me is not worthy of Me
Leave your family forever
Family always comes first
mc.why: Jesus said anyone loving father, mother, son, or daughter more than Him is not worthy of Him — God must hold first place even over family.

mc.stem: In the lesson, what was the real point of God asking Abraham to offer Isaac?
options: God wanted Isaac to die
To punish Abraham
To discover where Abraham's first love lay; God never meant the knife to fall
To test Isaac's obedience
mc.why: God stayed Abraham's hand; the point was never Isaac's death but revealing that Abraham loved God even more than his son.

mc.stem: How did Mary Welch answer the king's offer to free her imprisoned husband?
options: She promised he would never preach again
She offered the king money
She agreed to leave Scotland
She held up her apron and said she'd rather have her husband's head in it than make such a promise
mc.why: The king would free Welch if Mary promised he'd never preach again; she refused — she loved her husband, but she loved God more.

mc.stem: What did Jesus tell the rich young ruler, and why could he not do it?
options: To sell what he had and give to the poor; money had become his god
To pray more; he was too busy
To join the disciples; he feared travel
To keep the law; he had broken it
mc.why: Jesus told him to sell all and give to the poor; he could not, because wealth had become his god, claiming his time and heart.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, what is the basic question about our money?
options: How can we earn more?
Who really owns what we have — is it mine, or God's?
How little can we give?
How do we avoid taxes?
mc.why: The basic question is ownership: if it is mine I use it one way, if it is God's another. Scripture says all belongs to God, and the tithe is His.

mc.stem: What did the Brazilian family's tithed cattle demonstrate?
options: That they wanted to start a business
That cattle are valuable in Brazil
That they loved God more than money, though they had never seen a church
That they distrusted the missionaries
mc.why: Having only a Bible and no church, the family still set aside a tenth for years — proving they loved God more than money.

mc.stem: What three-word instruction from Hebrews 12:2 sums up the Christian life in the lesson?
options: Work for Jesus
Fear the Lord
Give to God
Looking unto Jesus
mc.why: Hebrews 12:2 — 'looking unto Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith' — sums up the whole Christian life: keep looking to Him.

mc.stem: The lesson compares losing sight of God to which children's game?
options: A staring game where the first to blink loses
Hide and seek
Tag
Leapfrog
mc.why: Like a staring game, we 'blink' in our spiritual life — losing sight of the Lord and looking somewhere else.

mc.stem: How is David used as 'a man that blinked'?
options: He doubted God before Goliath
He looked away from God amid power and praise, leading to his fall with Bathsheba
He refused to become king
He never sinned
mc.why: David trusted God against Goliath, but as king he looked away amid power and praise; that drifting gaze led to his fall with Bathsheba.

mc.stem: What does the Charles Spurgeon story illustrate about looking to Jesus?
options: That only adults can be saved
That preaching must be eloquent
That it is never too early to begin looking to Jesus
That bad weather hinders conversion
mc.why: A lay preacher pressed 'Look unto Me' on a miserable 15-year-old — the boy was Spurgeon. It is never too early to look to Jesus.

mc.stem: What does the B. H. Carroll story add to the Spurgeon story?
options: That conversion requires good weather
That bitter men cannot be saved
That only the young respond
That it is never too late to trust in Jesus, regardless of how one has lived
mc.why: Carroll, godless and embittered, looked up once and forever and became a great man of God — it is never too late to trust Jesus.

fill.prompt: Answering the lawyer, Jesus reached back to the ____, the confession every faithful Jew recited daily from Deuteronomy 6.

The second condition is that this is a love of ____: no gift may become as important to us as the Giver.
The motto "Called to serve," taken first, is wrong: we are first called to ____.

sa.prompt: Explain the setting of Matthew 22:34-38 and why Jesus' answer moves the question to the heart.
sa.model: An expert in the law asked Jesus which was the greatest commandment, and the text says he asked to test Him, not to learn, since the rabbis loved to trap a teacher over the ranking of the commands. Jesus did not hesitate but reached back to the Shema of Deuteronomy 6 and named love for God with all the heart, soul, and mind as the first and greatest. That answer moves the whole question off the surface of outward rule-keeping and drives it down to the heart: the greatest thing God requires is not a performance He can audit but an affection given with the whole self. Love is the foundation of the Christian life, and every other command grows from it.

sa.prompt: What does it mean that love for God must be 'total,' and how is the basis of obedience?
sa.model: Jesus means a total love, for Christianity is a religion of the whole person: we are to love God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind, every faculty bent toward Him. The three are not separate compartments but three angles on one undivided self, leaving no part exempt. This total love is the very basis of obedience, because when we love God with everything we strive with everything within us to do what He wants, and obedience becomes the natural leaning of a life rather than a demand from outside. The lesson pictures it as a tree by the seashore: just as it is bent over the years by the prevailing wind, the whole Christian is meant to be bent by the will of God.

sa.prompt: Explain what it means that this is a love of 'degree' and the danger it warns against.
sa.model: Besides being total, the love Jesus commands is a love of degree, meaning it concerns how much we love God compared with everything else. God has given us many good things to enjoy in this world, and they are genuine gifts, not evils. But we must always guard the order of our loves so that no gift, however good, ever becomes as important to us as the Giver. The danger is that a worthy thing can quietly take first place in the heart. If we love God with all our heart, soul, and mind, then nothing is allowed to come between us and Him, and every other love is kept in its proper, lesser place.

sa.prompt: Explain the lesson's correction of 'Called to serve' and how Enoch models the better way.
sa.model: We often pick up the idea that all God wants is for us to work ourselves to death, so we become guilt-ridden and miserable, and we even hang 'Called to serve' over our doors. The lesson corrects this: we are not first called to serve at all, but to love; service is good but must grow out of love rather than replace it, or religion becomes joyless duty. Enoch models the better way. Almost all Scripture records of him is that he walked with God and God took him — a life whose whole commentary is fellowship with God. He fulfilled the purpose we were all made for, since God created us for fellowship with Himself, and so the searching question is whether our own life would read, 'He walked with God.'

sa.prompt: According to the lesson, what is most likely the greatest sin, and why is it the one we overlook?
sa.model: We all keep a private list of sins, with murder, adultery, theft, and blasphemy near the top, because we feel their weight instinctively. But as Peter Lord points out, the greatest sin is most likely tied to the greatest commandment, for to commit the greatest sin is to break the greatest commandment. Since loving God with everything is the first and greatest command, failing to love Him is the first and greatest sin. It is the one we overlook precisely because it never makes our list; we measure sin by dramatic outward acts and miss the quiet failure to give God the fellowship and love He most desires. God is not chiefly after our work or money but our love.

sa.prompt: How does the Abraham-and-Isaac account teach loving God more than family?
sa.model: Jesus said anyone who loves father, mother, son, or daughter more than Him is not worthy of Him, because even a good love like family can take first place in the heart. Abraham faced this in its sharpest form when God asked him to offer Isaac, the son he had waited a lifetime for. He loved the boy more than his own life, yet he loved God more, and in heart and intent he gave his son to the Lord. God never meant the knife to fall and stayed Abraham's hand; the point was never Isaac's death but the discovery of where Abraham's first love lay. The same test comes to us in quieter forms, when family attachments would hold us back from full obedience to God.

sa.prompt: Use the rich young ruler to explain loving God more than money, and the question of ownership.
sa.model: Jesus said we cannot serve God and money, and He proved it with the rich young ruler, who sensed something was missing yet could not obey when told to sell what he had and give to the poor. Money had quietly become his god, claiming his time, thought, and energy. The story presses the question of ownership on us: who really owns what we hold? If it is mine I use it one way; if it is God's, another. Scripture says the earth, the cattle, even the birds belong to God, who owns all we have, and He says the tithe is the Lord's, so to withhold it is to rob God. How we hold our money quietly reveals whether we love the gift or the Giver.

sa.prompt: What does the Brazilian family illustrate about loving God more than money?
sa.model: A blacksmith in the interior of Brazil was converted by an open-air evangelist, given a Bible, and went home and taught his family from it for years. When Baptist workers finally found them, they discovered the family had been setting aside a tenth of their cattle earnings the whole time, simply because the Scriptures said the tithe belonged to God. They had never even seen a church, so they were not imitating other believers or seeking approval; they obeyed because they took God's Word at face value. With their herd they proved that they loved God more than money, illustrating that real love for God shows itself in how we hold our possessions, even when no one is watching.

sa.prompt: Explain Hebrews 12:2 and how David shows the danger of 'blinking.'
sa.model: Hebrews 12:2 sums up the Christian life in three words, 'looking unto Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith.' The instruction is simple but hard to keep, and the lesson compares losing sight of God to a staring game in which we 'blink' and look somewhere else, usually toward the world's glitter and desires. David is the great example. As a shepherd boy his eyes were so fixed on God that, with a sling and his faith, he felled the giant Goliath. But as king, amid power and praise, he looked away from God, and one evening his gaze drifted to his neighbor's wife and he fell. Had his eyes stayed on the Lord, he could have escaped the temptation, and so the Christian struggle is largely about where we are looking.

sa.prompt: Using Spurgeon and B. H. Carroll, explain why it is never too early or too late to look to Jesus.
sa.model: If the whole of the Christian life is learning to look to Jesus, two encouragements follow. First, it is never too early: a lay preacher in a snowbound English chapel could only repeat 'Look unto Me, and be saved,' and pressed it on a miserable fifteen-year-old who became Charles Spurgeon, so a young heart that learns to look has the best of beginnings. Second, it is never too late: B. H. Carroll, godless and embittered and crippled by war, was dragged unwillingly to church, and though the sermon left him empty, at its end Christ seemed to stand before him calling, and he looked up once and forever to become a great man of God. Whether early or late, the command and the door are the same — love God and keep looking to Him.
